$comment: Bauhaus art data. Lengths are in units of a 400 x 400 artboard (multiply by artboard short side / 400), or given as percentages. Colours are roles only; hex values always come from the product's Wada combination. Numbers are rules of thumb distilled from 1920s Bauhaus print (research.md 2), not measurements of specific works.

line.$comment: There is no drawn line. 'Line' means bars and rules: filled rectangles with square ends, in three fixed weights.

heavy.use: Structural bars: masthead, the diagonal, blocks that anchor type.

medium.use: Dividers between headline and body, underlines, arrows.

hairline.use: Thin rules that extend a heavy bar or frame a column.

rules: Bars run at 0°, 90° or along the piece's one diagonal.
A bar starts or ends on a grid line, a form's edge, or bleeds off the sheet; never stops in empty space.
Never dashed, dotted, outlined or tapered. No strokes around forms.

shape.$comment: The elementary forms. Exact geometry, flat fill, no outline.

forms.use: The usual focal form. One large circle per piece at most.
A stable block; also the basis of image boxes.
Equilateral or right-angled with the hypotenuse on the 45° diagonal. Points direction and energy.
Long rectangle (length at least 6 x width). Structure and rhythm.
Horizon, rising, a door or arch. Cut on a grid line.
A corner turned, a fan; sits in the corner of a square.

sizes.$comment: Diameter or side as a share of the artboard's short side.
sizes.ratio: Each size step is about 2-3 x the next one down; avoid forms of nearly equal size.

shape.overlap: Forms may overlap; where they do, the upper form covers the lower completely (no transparency, no blend modes). At least one overlap per piece ties the forms together.
rules: Exact circles, squares and triangles; no rounded corners, no freeform paths.
The accent colour fills one form only: the focal form.

corners.$comment: Square corners for layout and UI around the art. Circles are allowed for round buttons and circular image crops. Pixels at 1x for screens.

use.button: xs (square), or pill only for a circular icon button
use.input: xs, with a medium-weight bottom rule instead of a box
use.card: xs, separated by rules rather than boxes
use.image: xs, or a full circle crop

corners.nested: All corners square, so nesting needs no adjustment.
corners.print: Square corners on every image box and panel.

grid.$comment: The construction grid. Everything snaps to it.
grid.module: On posters the 8 columns form square modules; forms take 1, 2, 4 or 6 modules across.
grid.diagonal: One diagonal axis per piece, at 45° or -45°. Bars, triangle edges and rotated text on the diagonal all share it.
grid.verticalText: Text rotated -90° (reading bottom to top) along a margin or bar; at most one vertical line per piece.

composition.grid: 8 columns on posters, 12 on screen; forms and text blocks start and end on column lines.
composition.balance: Asymmetric. The focal form sits on the left or right third, or bleeds off one edge by 10-25% of its diameter; type sits on the opposite side or below.

placements.use: Focal circle bleeds off the right or top edge; headline bottom-left. The default poster.
Everything hangs on the one 45° axis: a heavy bar, a triangle edge, sometimes a line of type.
A heavy bar or a colour block splits the sheet into two unequal fields (about 1:2); image in one, type in the other.
A hard-cropped black-and-white photo with the headline and bars set against it; the photo replaces the focal form.

composition.pairing: Form and headline are a pair: the form shows the idea in geometry (a sun, a door, a direction); the headline says what it means for the reader (W5).
rules: One focal form per piece; it carries the accent colour.
Never centre the composition; never centre text.
At least one form bleeds off an edge or one bar runs the full width: the sheet's edge is part of the composition.
Keep at least one margin between type and the nearest form, except where type deliberately sits on a bar.

palette.$comment: Share of the visible area for each colour role. Colours come from the product's Wada combination; black and white are always available.

ground.from: combination bg (or Wada White when the combination's bg is a strong primary used as the accent)

paper.use: Forms and type on dark or saturated grounds.

method: Start from what the product needs to say, then pick a combination with a strong primary (red, yellow or blue) from recommendedCombinations.
Prefer combinations whose light-mode inkUse is 'body', so type in the text role passes AA.
Decide the ground first: a light ground (cream, white, grey, yellow) for calm, information-heavy pieces; a red, blue or black ground for one-message posters.
Give the focal form the accent; give everything else black (or white on a dark ground).
Use the full red-yellow-blue triad only with combination 154, and then in unequal areas (about 60 : 25 : 10 by area).

recommendedCombinations.why: The classic primary triad in one Wada combination: yellow ground, blue accent, carmine type (AA).
Yellow and black, the strongest contrast pair (15.9:1); pure poster energy.
Red and black, the core pair of Bauhaus printing; white type on carmine passes AA.
Grey ground with a red focal form and black bars: the most restrained, very readable.
Yellow ground, carmine accent and black type; the green is reserved as a small support form or left out.
Yellow and deep blue, both primaries; blue type on yellow at 8.3:1.
Cream ground like unbleached paper with black: the calm, bookish Bauhaus (catalogues, Bauhaus books).
Deep red on cream: printed-matter warmth with AA type in carmine red.
Red and blue, like the 1923 catalogue cover's lettering; use white type, since the pair itself is decorative only.
A warmer, shifted triad (orange-red, orange-yellow, violet) for products that need the structure without the textbook primaries.

rules: No gradients, shadows, glows, tints or transparency effects.
Text colour on the ground uses the combination's text role, or black or white, whichever passes AA.
The accent never goes on type, except one short word or numeral set very large.

halftone.use: Only inside photographs (black-and-white or duotone with the accent), as printed halftone. Never as shading on geometric forms.

photomontage.$comment: Typophoto: photographs as part of the typographic construction.
photomontage.treatment: Black and white, or duotone (black plus the combination's accent). High contrast; deep blacks.
photomontage.angles: Viewpoints from directly above or steeply below; flat frontal shots only for objects.
rules: A photo takes the place of a form, not an extra layer on top of everything.
Bars and type may cross a photo edge; nothing is placed inside a photo except type on a solid bar.
No colour photographs with their own palette; no soft vignettes.

vocabulary.$comment: Elementary forms and what they can say. Pair one form with the product's message, or build a simple sign from two forms.

symbols.build: three or four bars of decreasing length
one lowercase letter set at 50-80% of the sheet height

means: a price, date, year or count as the image
symbols.build: one numeral or number, as on Bayer's 1923 banknotes
a black-and-white photo cropped to a circle or square

avoid.why: A specific historical mark; copying it reads as pastiche or trademark use.

avoid.symbol: Kandinsky's yellow triangle, red square, blue circle as a set
avoid.why: The most worn Bauhaus cliché; and the pairing was contested even at the time (research.md 2.3). Use colour by role, not by Kandinsky's code.

avoid.symbol: Mondrian-style black grid with coloured rectangles
avoid.why: That is De Stijl, a different movement; mixing them looks generic.

avoid.symbol: the word 'Bauhaus', German slogans, 'form follows function'
avoid.why: Decoration with words; the slogan is Louis Sullivan's, not the Bauhaus's.
Cliché; the precision should be in the construction, not the subject.

avoid.symbol: ITC Bauhaus or other 'Bauhaus' novelty fonts
avoid.why: A 1975 commercial interpretation; it reads as theme-party Bauhaus.

method.$comment: Construction method: how to get from a message to a composition.
recipe: Write the one message in a sentence (W1).
Choose the one form that carries it (circle = sun, plate, focus; triangle = direction; half circle = arch, loaf, sunrise). Make it the focal form, 45-75% of the short side.
Choose the diagonal or decide there is none. If there is one, put a heavy bar or a triangle edge on it.
Place the focal form on a third or bleeding off an edge; put the headline in the opposite field, on the grid.
Add one or two secondary forms or bars that link the focal form to the headline (overlap, alignment, a bar that runs from one to the other).
Colour: accent on the focal form, black on bars and type, everything else ground.
Squint test: at thumbnail size, the focal form and the headline should be the only two things you see.

examples.idea: a loaf on a counter: fresh bread, every morning
rising steps: progress you can see
the price or date is the message

checklist: One message; one focal form in the accent colour.
Only circle, square, triangle, bars (and half or quarter circles); at most five forms.
Angles 0°, 90° and at most one 45° diagonal.
Asymmetric; at least one form or bar meets the sheet's edge.
Ground 45-65%, black 10-25%, accent 10-25%, support 10% or less.
Bars in the three fixed weights; no outlines, no rounded corners, no gradients.
Type on the grid, left-aligned, bold sans headline, three sizes at most.
